pos: v. (past tense and past participle of lead; rendering Hebrew nahah and yalak, Greek ago)
etymology: Old English lædan, to cause to go; the past form of lead. The word of a hand upon the way — someone else chose the road.
biblical_def: To be led is to be brought along a way by another. God led Israel by the pillar and not by the short road: “God led the people about, through the way of the wilderness” (Exo 13:18), and “led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee” (Deu 8:2). Christ was “led up of the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted” (Mat 4:1) and “led as a sheep to the slaughter” (Act 8:32). The Christian is defined by the same passive: “as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God” (Rom 8:14); “if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law” (Gal 5:18). The ascended Christ “led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men” (Eph 4:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives led as the past tense and participle of lead: conducted, guided, drawn.
webster_full: LED, pret. and pp. of lead. Conducted; guided; drawn; allured.
scriptures: Rom 8:14
For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.
Gal 5:18
But if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law.
Deu 8:2

And thou shalt remember all the way which the LORD thy God led thee these forty years in the wilderness, to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart, whether thou wouldest keep his commandments, or no.
Act 8:32
The place of the scripture which he read was this, He was led as a sheep to the slaughter; and like a lamb dumb before his shearer, so opened he not his mouth:
Eph 4:8
Wherefore he saith, When he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive, and gave gifts unto men.
But God led the people about, through the way of the wilderness of the Red sea: and the children of Israel went up harnessed out of the land of Egypt.
corruption_summary: Being led by the Spirit is claimed for private impressions, and Paul uses the phrase for the mortifying of sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 8:14 stands at the end of an argument, not at the start of a mystery. The verse before it reads, “if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live,” and then: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God.” The leading Paul has in view is visible in a killed sin, not felt in an inward nudge. Galatians 5:18 does the same work — “if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law” — and the sentence runs straight on into the works of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit. Being led has a direction, and the direction is holiness. The man who says the Spirit led him into what Scripture forbids has named the wrong leader.

The passive voice is the point of the word. Christ was led to the slaughter; Israel was led through the wilderness; and every one of the forty years was chosen for them, “to humble thee, and to prove thee, to know what was in thine heart.” Exodus 13:17 records that God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, “although that was near,” lest the people repent when they saw war. The direct road was refused on purpose. Those who complain that God's path is indirect have Exodus 13 against them: the short way was the way that would have destroyed them.

Ephesians 4:8 turns the word to triumph. Psalm 68 pictured a conqueror ascending with his captives in train; Paul says the ascended Christ “led captivity captive” — the captor taken captive — and distributed the spoil as gifts to the church. The One who was led away bound to Caiaphas (Mat 26:57) and led away to be crucified (John 19:16) is the same One who now leads the whole procession.
roots_summary: Hebrew nahah (H5148), to guide; yalak in the causative (H3212), to cause to walk; Greek ago (G71), to lead, bring; aichmaloteuo (G162), to lead captive.
roots_lines: Hebrew nahah (H5148) — to lead, guide; Exodus 13:17, 13:21, Psalm 23:3, Psalm 78:14.
Hebrew yalak, hiphil (H3212) — to cause to go, to lead; Deuteronomy 8:2, 8:15, 29:5.
Greek ago (G71) — to lead, bring, carry; Luke 4:1, Acts 8:32, Romans 8:14, Galatians 5:18.
Greek aichmaloteuo (G162) — to lead captive; Ephesians 4:8, quoting Psalm 68:18.
usage: “As many as are led by the Spirit of God” — sonship shown in the leading, and the leading shown in a mortified sin.
“He led captivity captive” — the Ascension as a triumph.
“He was led as a sheep to the slaughter” — Isaiah 53 read aloud in a chariot.

pos: v. (third person singular of lie: to recline, remain, be situated; rendering Hebrew rabats and shakab, Greek keimai)
etymology: Old English licgan, to lie down. The Authorized Version's -eth form of lie in the sense of resting along a surface; the AV also has the other lie, to speak falsely (“lieth concerning it,” Lev 6:3), a different word by descent.
biblical_def: Something lieth when it rests where it has been laid. “Sin lieth at the door” (Gen 4:7) — the Hebrew is the crouching of an animal. “The whole world lieth in wickedness” (1Jn 5:19) — John's verb is a posture, the world lying in the wicked one as a man lies in a bed. Job says, “man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more” (Job 14:12). Paul measures a duty by it: “as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18). And the last city “lieth foursquare” (Rev 21:16). Of the sick: “my servant lieth at home sick of the palsy” (Mat 8:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lie as to be extended on a surface, to rest; to be situated; to remain in a state or condition.
webster_full: LIE, v.i. To be in a horizontal position, or nearly so, and to rest on any thing lengthwise; to rest in a reclining posture.
2. To be situated; as, the land lies on the east.
3. To remain in a state or condition; to be laid up; to lie in wait; to lie at the mercy of.
scriptures: Gen 4:7
If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.
And we know that we are of God, and the whole world lieth in wickedness.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
So man lieth down, and riseth not: till the heavens be no more, they shall not awake, nor be raised out of their sleep.
And the city lieth foursquare, and the length is as large as the breadth: and he measured the city with the reed, twelve thousand furlongs. The length and the breadth and the height of it are equal.
Psa 41:8
An evil disease, say they, cleaveth fast unto him: and now that he lieth he shall rise up no more.
corruption_summary: The world lying in wickedness is softened into a world with problems, and Genesis 4:7 is preached as a promise of willpower.
corruption_paragraphs: First John 5:19 is a verse about position. “We know that we are of God, and the whole world lieth in wickedness” — two places, no third. The world is not described as struggling, drifting, or mixed; it lies in the wicked one the way a body lies in a bed, because that is where it rests. Modern religion prefers a world that is basically well-meaning and occasionally mistaken, and it reads John's verb as a mood. John meant a posture, and the only way out of the posture is to be “of God,” which is birth, not improvement.

Genesis 4:7 is God's warning to Cain before the first murder: “if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him.” The verb is the crouching of a beast (the same word describes Issachar “couching down between two burdens,” Gen 49:14), and the verse is commonly preached as a promise of mastery: sin is waiting, but you can rule it. Cain is the answer to that reading. The man warned went straight out into the field and did it. The command exposes the inability; it does not confer the ability. What masters sin is not resolve but grace — “sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace” (Rom 6:14).

Romans 12:18 gives the word its honest limit. “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” — Paul does not promise peace with everyone, because peace takes two. He commands everything that lies in the believer's part and leaves the other man's part where it lies.
roots_summary: Hebrew rabats (H7257), to crouch, couch; shakab (H7901), to lie down; Greek keimai (G2749), to lie, be laid.
roots_lines: Hebrew rabats (H7257) — to crouch as an animal; Genesis 4:7, Genesis 49:9, 49:14.
Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down, to lie with; Job 14:12, Psalm 41:8, Leviticus 15:4.
Greek keimai (G2749) — to lie, be laid, be set; 1 John 5:19, Revelation 21:16, Luke 2:12.
Greek ballo, passive (G906) — laid, thrown down; Matthew 8:6, “lieth at home sick of the palsy.”
usage: “Sin lieth at the door” — a beast couching, and a man who did not rule it.
“The whole world lieth in wickedness” — a posture, not a mood.
“As much as lieth in you” — the measure of your own part in peace.

pos: v. (third person singular of see; rendering Hebrew ra'ah, Greek blepo and theoreo)
etymology: Old English sēon. The AV's third-person form of see, kept for the one verse the corpus most needs it in: the LORD seeth not as man seeth.
biblical_def: God seeth what man cannot. “The LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1Sa 16:7). He “seeth under the whole heaven” (Job 28:24). Christ builds three commands on it: alms, prayer, and fasting are for “thy Father which seeth in secret” (Mat 6:4, 6, 18). The Son does “what he seeth the Father do” (John 5:19), and the world cannot receive the Spirit “because it seeth him not” (John 14:17). The elders in Ezekiel's vision say the opposite creed in the dark: “The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth” (Eze 8:12). John turns the word on the Christian: “whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?” (1Jn 3:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines see as to perceive by the eye; to observe; to discern; to understand; to attend or regard.
webster_full: SEE, v.t. To perceive by the eye; to have knowledge of the existence and apparent qualities of objects by the organs of sight.
2. To observe; to note or notice; to know; to regard or look to.
3. To discover; to descry; to understand.
scriptures: But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
Mat 6:4
That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.
John 5:19

Then answered Jesus and said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, The Son can do nothing of himself, but what he seeth the Father do: for what things soever he doeth, these also doeth the Son likewise.
But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?
Eze 8:12

Then said he unto me, Son of man, hast thou seen what the ancients of the house of Israel do in the dark, every man in the chambers of his imagery? for they say, The LORD seeth us not; the LORD hath forsaken the earth.
John 14:17
Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you.
corruption_summary: God's seeing the heart is quoted as comfort for the unrepentant, when it was spoken to pass a man over.
corruption_paragraphs: “God knows my heart” is the modern use of 1 Samuel 16:7, and it is offered as an excuse: the conduct was poor, but the heart was good, and God sees the heart. The verse was spoken to disqualify Eliab. Samuel looked at the eldest son and was sure; the LORD looked at the heart and refused him. That God seeth the heart is the reason to fear, not the reason to relax — “the heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the LORD search the heart” (Jer 17:9–10). A man who appeals from his conduct to his heart has appealed to the harsher court.

Ezekiel 8 shows the practical atheism of religious men. Seventy elders of Israel stand in the dark with censers, every man in the chambers of his imagery, and their creed is one sentence: “The LORD seeth us not.” Every hidden sin is a small Ezekiel 8; it can only be done by first believing, for the length of the act, that God does not see. Matthew 6 turns the same fact into promise. The alms given, the prayer prayed, and the fast kept where no man sees are seen — “thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.” The one audience never misses a performance, and it is the only one that pays.

First John 3:17 forbids the spiritualising of the word. The man who seeth his brother have need and shuts up his bowels of compassion has seen, and seeing was the whole obligation. Love that has seen a need and done nothing is not love that is waiting for guidance; John asks how the love of God dwelleth in it at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'ah (H7200), to see, look, regard; Greek blepo (G991), to look at; theoreo (G2334), to behold, perceive.
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, regard; 1 Samuel 16:7, Job 28:24, Genesis 16:13, “Thou God seest me.”
Greek blepo (G991) — to look, see; Matthew 6:4, 6:6, 6:18, John 5:19.
Greek theoreo (G2334) — to behold, discern; John 14:17, 14:19, 1 John 3:17.
usage: “The LORD seeth not as man seeth” — Eliab passed over.
“Thy Father which seeth in secret” — the audience of one.
“The LORD seeth us not” — the elders' creed in the dark.

pos: v. (third person singular of die; rendering Hebrew muth, Greek apothnesko and teleutao)
etymology: Old Norse deyja, through Middle English dien. The AV form carries the three great sentences on death: man dieth, the worm dieth not, and Christ dieth no more.
biblical_def: Man dieth: “But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?” (Job 14:10). “When a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish” (Pro 11:7); “when he dieth he shall carry nothing away” (Psa 49:17). Christ said three times in one breath of hell, “Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched” (Mar 9:44, 46, 48). And Paul: “Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him” (Rom 6:9). Even the Christian's dying is not his own: “no man dieth to himself” (Rom 14:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines die as to be deprived of respiration, of the circulation of blood, and other bodily functions, and rendered incapable of resuscitation; to expire; to perish.
webster_full: DIE, v.i. To be deprived of respiration, of the circulation of the blood, and other bodily functions, and rendered incapable of resuscitation, as animals, either by natural decay, by disease, or by violence; to cease to live; to expire; to decease; to perish.
2. To be lost; to perish or come to nothing; as, let the secret die in your own breast.
3. To sink; to faint. Also, to languish with affection.
scriptures: Rom 6:9
Knowing that Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more; death hath no more dominion over him.
Mar 9:44
Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.
Rom 14:7
For none of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself.
But man dieth, and wasteth away: yea, man giveth up the ghost, and where is he?
Pro 11:7
When a wicked man dieth, his expectation shall perish: and the hope of unjust men perisheth.
For when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him.
corruption_summary: Christ is said never to have taught eternal punishment, and He said the worm dieth not three times in one paragraph.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 9:44, 46, and 48 are one sentence said three times: “Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.” The claim that Jesus never taught an unending punishment has to get past the fact that the plainest teacher who ever lived chose to repeat this, and that the phrase is a quotation of the last verse of Isaiah, where the carcases of the transgressors are looked upon by all flesh. The annihilationist reads “dieth not” as poetry. The Lord attached it to a hand, a foot, and an eye, and told men to cut them off rather than go there. Nobody amputates for a metaphor.

Romans 6:9 guards the resurrection from being shrunk to a resuscitation. Lazarus came out of the tomb and died again; the widow's son and Jairus's daughter were raised and later buried. Christ “dieth no more,” because His death was “once” (Heb 9:26–28) and finished what it came to do. Death had dominion over Him for three days by His own consent; it has none now, and the believer's death is therefore a death Christ has already been through and come out of.

Romans 14:7 makes dying a stewardship. “None of us liveth to himself, and no man dieth to himself” — the modern claim to own one's own death, to end it on one's own terms, is answered by a verse that will not let a Christian own even that. “Whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's.”
roots_summary: Hebrew muth (H4191), to die; gava (H1478), to expire, give up the ghost; Greek apothnesko (G599), to die off; teleutao (G5053), to come to an end.
roots_lines: Hebrew muth (H4191) — to die; Job 14:10, Proverbs 11:7, Psalm 49:17, Ecclesiastes 3:19.
Hebrew gava (H1478) — to expire, breathe out; Job 14:10, “giveth up the ghost.”
Greek apothnesko (G599) — to die; Romans 6:9, Romans 14:7–8, 1 Corinthians 15:22.
Greek teleutao (G5053) — to end, to die; Mark 9:44, 46, 48, “their worm dieth not.”
usage: “Dieth no more” — resurrection, not resuscitation.
“Where their worm dieth not” — said three times, attached to a hand, a foot, and an eye.
“No man dieth to himself” — even the last act is stewardship.

pos: v. (past tense of overthrow; rendering Hebrew haphak and na'ar, Greek katastrepho and anastrepho)
etymology: Over + throw: to turn a thing upside down. The Hebrew behind Sodom's overthrow, haphak, is the ordinary word for turning something over.
biblical_def: God overthrew Sodom: “he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities” (Gen 19:25), and the sentence became Scripture's standing measure of judgment — Babylon shall be “as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” (Isa 13:19; Jer 50:40), and Israel is told, “I have overthrown some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet have ye not returned unto me” (Amo 4:11). He “overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea” (Exo 14:27), which Psalm 136 sings as mercy: “But overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red sea: for his mercy endureth for ever” (Psa 136:15). In the temple Christ “overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves” (Mat 21:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overthrow as to turn upside down; to throw down; to demolish; to defeat; to subvert; to ruin.
webster_full: OVERTHROW, v.t. To turn upside down.
2. To throw down; to demolish; as, to overthrow a building.
3. To ruin; to subvert; to destroy; as, to overthrow the state.
4. To defeat; to conquer; as, to overthrow an army.
scriptures: And he overthrew those cities, and all the plain, and all the inhabitants of the cities, and that which grew upon the ground.
Amo 4:11
I have overthrown some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, and ye were as a firebrand plucked out of the burning: yet have ye not returned unto me, saith the LORD.
But overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red sea: for his mercy endureth for ever.
And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves,
And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldees' excellency, shall be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah.

And Moses stretched forth his hand over the sea, and the sea returned to his strength when the morning appeared; and the Egyptians fled against it; and the LORD overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea.
corruption_summary: Sodom's overthrow is retold as a judgment on inhospitality, and the psalm that sings it as mercy is left unsung.
corruption_paragraphs: Sodom is the Bible's own unit of judgment. Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, Peter (2Pe 2:6), and Jude (v. 7) all reach for the same overthrow when they need to say what God does to a city. The modern retelling makes Sodom's sin inhospitality, quoting Ezekiel 16:49 — pride, fulness of bread, abundance of idleness — and stopping before verse 50, “and committed abomination before me: therefore I took them away as I saw good.” Jude names the abomination: “giving themselves over to fornication, and going after strange flesh.” Ezekiel's list is not a substitute for Genesis 19; it is the soil Genesis 19 grew in.

The same verb turns up in God's own heart. In Hosea 11:8 the LORD asks, “how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Zeboim?” — two of the cities of the plain — and answers, “mine heart is turned within me.” The word for turned is haphak, the word for Sodom's overthrow. Rather than overthrow Israel, God is overthrown within Himself; the repentings are kindled together. That is the Old Testament's shape of the cross.

Psalm 136 sets the overthrow of Pharaoh between two refrains of “for his mercy endureth for ever.” Judgment on the enemy is mercy to the redeemed, and a theology that cannot sing verse 15 has not understood verse 1. Matthew 21:12 adds the last correction: the meek Christ overthrew furniture. The zeal was for His Father's house (John 2:17), not for His own wounded honour, and the man who quotes it to bless his temper has borrowed the scourge without the cause.
roots_summary: Hebrew haphak (H2015), to turn, overturn; na'ar (H5287), to shake off; Greek katastrepho (G2690), to overturn; anastrepho (G390), to turn over.
roots_lines: Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn, overturn, overthrow; Genesis 19:25, Deuteronomy 29:23, Amos 4:11, Hosea 11:8.
Hebrew na'ar (H5287) — to shake off, toss; Exodus 14:27, Psalm 136:15.
Greek katastrepho (G2690) — to turn over, upset; Matthew 21:12, Mark 11:15.
Greek anastrepho (G390) — to overturn; John 2:15, the tables in the temple.
usage: “As God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” — the standing measure of judgment.
“Overthrew Pharaoh and his host in the Red sea: for his mercy endureth for ever” — judgment sung as mercy.
“Overthrew the tables of the moneychangers” — zeal for the house, not for the self.

pos: v. (past tense of drive; also n., a herd on the move; rendering Hebrew garash and nashab, Greek ekballo)
etymology: Old English drifan, to drive, push forward. The noun drove is the thing driven — Jacob's flocks going ahead of him toward Esau.
biblical_def: The word opens the Bible's exile: “So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword” (Gen 3:24). Abram “drove them away” when the fowls came down on the covenant sacrifice (Gen 15:11). Caleb “drove thence the three sons of Anak” (Jos 15:14). Habakkuk's God “beheld, and drove asunder the nations” (Hab 3:6). In the temple Christ made a scourge of small cords and “drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen” (John 2:15). As a noun: Jacob sent his gifts to Esau “every drove by themselves” (Gen 32:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives drove as the past tense of drive, and as a noun, a collection of cattle driven; a crowd of people in motion.
webster_full: DROVE, pret. of drive.
DROVE, n. A collection of cattle driven; a number of animals, as oxen, sheep or swine, driven in a body.
2. A crowd of people in motion.
scriptures: Gen 3:24
So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.
John 2:15
And when he had made a scourge of small cords, he drove them all out of the temple, and the sheep, and the oxen; and poured out the changers' money, and overthrew the tables;
And when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away.
And Caleb drove thence the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai, the children of Anak.
Hab 3:6
He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting.
And he delivered them into the hand of his servants, every drove by themselves; and said unto his servants, Pass over before me, and put a space betwixt drove and drove.
corruption_summary: The expulsion from Eden is read as cruelty, when the verse before it shows the driving out as mercy.
corruption_paragraphs: “So he drove out the man” is read as the harsh end of a gentle story. Genesis 3:22 gives the reason: “lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever” — live for ever, that is, in the state he had just fallen into. An immortal sinner is the one thing the garden must not produce. The driving out is the first act of redemption after the promise of verse 15: the way to the tree is kept, not destroyed, and Revelation 22:14 shows men coming back to it by a door the sword no longer bars.

Genesis 15:11 is a small verse about a large discipline. God had told Abram to lay out the sacrifice; the sun had not gone down; the covenant had not yet been cut; and the fowls came down upon the carcases. “Abram drove them away.” Between the promise and its performance there is a season in which the believer's whole work is to keep the birds off what God has appointed, until the smoking furnace passes between the pieces. Prayer, patience, and the plain refusal to let the thing be picked apart — that is what driving the fowls away looks like.

John 2:15 stands next to John 3. The Lord who received Nicodemus by night with the gentlest teaching in the Gospel had, a few verses earlier, driven men and cattle out of the temple with a scourge. Meekness is not the absence of force; it is force under command. The corruption runs both ways: a Christ too soft to drive anyone out, and a Christian who quotes the scourge for his own irritation.
roots_summary: Hebrew garash (H1644), to drive out, expel; nashab (H5380), to blow away, drive off; eder (H5739), a flock, drove; Greek ekballo (G1544), to cast out.
roots_lines: Hebrew garash (H1644) — to drive out, cast out; Genesis 3:24, Exodus 2:17, Exodus 23:28.
Hebrew nashab (H5380) — to blow, drive away; Genesis 15:11.
Hebrew eder (H5739) — a flock, herd, drove; Genesis 32:16, 32:19, 33:8.
Greek ekballo (G1544) — to cast out, drive out; John 2:15, Mark 1:12.
usage: “So he drove out the man” — expulsion with the way kept.
“Abram drove them away” — keeping the sacrifice until God came down to it.
“He drove them all out of the temple” — the meek Lord with a scourge.

pos: v. (to rest one's weight upon, to rely; also adj., thin, ill-fed; rendering Hebrew sha'an and daq)
etymology: Old English hleonian, to incline, recline. The adjective (thin) is a separate Old English word, hlæne; the AV has both, and Pharaoh's lean kine keep the second.
biblical_def: To lean is to put one's weight on a thing so that if it gives way, one falls. “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding” (Pro 3:5). Egypt is a bruised reed, “on which if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it” (2Ki 18:21). The hypocrite “shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand” (Job 8:15). Micah's corrupt rulers “yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us” (Mic 3:11). Samson asked to lean upon the pillars (Jdg 16:26). The adjective: “the lean and the ill favoured kine did eat up the first seven fat kine” (Gen 41:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lean as to deviate from an erect position and rest against something for support; to depend on for support; and, as an adjective, wanting flesh, thin, meager.
webster_full: LEAN, v.i. To deviate or move from a straight or perpendicular line; to incline; as, a column leans to the north.
2. To incline or bend against; to rest against or on something for support.
3. To depend on for support; as, to lean on the counsel of a friend.
LEAN, a. Wanting flesh; thin; meager; not fat; as a lean body.
scriptures: Pro 3:5
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.

Now, behold, thou trustest upon the staff of this bruised reed, even upon Egypt, on which if a man lean, it will go into his hand, and pierce it: so is Pharaoh king of Egypt unto all that trust on him.
Job 8:15
He shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand: he shall hold it fast, but it shall not endure.
Mic 3:11

The heads thereof judge for reward, and the priests thereof teach for hire, and the prophets thereof divine for money: yet will they lean upon the LORD, and say, Is not the LORD among us? none evil can come upon us.
And the lean and the ill favoured kine did eat up the first seven fat kine:
And Samson said unto the lad that held him by the hand, Suffer me that I may feel the pillars whereupon the house standeth, that I may lean upon them.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 3:5 is quoted against thinking, when it forbids leaning on the understanding, not using it.
corruption_paragraphs: “Lean not unto thine own understanding” is the anti-intellectual's favourite half-verse. The whole verse has a positive command first — “Trust in the LORD with all thine heart” — and the next verse a practice: “in all thy ways acknowledge him.” The understanding is not condemned; it is demoted from crutch to tool. A man uses a tool and rests on a crutch, and Solomon, who asked God for an understanding heart, is not telling his son to stop thinking. He is telling him where not to put his weight.

Micah 3:11 describes the false lean. Heads that judge for reward, priests that teach for hire, prophets that divine for money — “yet will they lean upon the LORD.” It is possible to lean on God as a superstition: to presume His presence while despising His law, and to make “Is not the LORD among us?” a charm against consequences. Micah's next verse is the answer: “Therefore shall Zion for your sake be plowed as a field.” Leaning on the LORD without obeying the LORD is leaning on a name.

Egypt is the Bible's picture of the world's help: a bruised reed that goes into the hand of the man who leans on it. Every alliance Judah made in that direction ended in the wound (Isa 30:1–3; 31:1), and the Assyrian who mocked the reed in 2 Kings 18 was, for once, telling the truth. Job 8:15 generalises it — “he shall lean upon his house, but it shall not stand” — and the only weight-bearing thing left in the Bible is the One Proverbs names first.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'an (H8172), to lean, rely, rest upon; daq (H1851), thin, lean; razeh (H7330), lean; Greek anakeimai (G345), to recline.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'an (H8172) — to lean, support oneself, rely; Proverbs 3:5, 2 Kings 18:21, Job 8:15, Micah 3:11, Judges 16:26.
Hebrew daq (H1851) — thin, lean; Genesis 41:19–20, the lean kine.
Hebrew razeh (H7330) — lean, thin; Numbers 13:20, Ezekiel 34:20.
Greek anakeimai (G345) — to recline at table; John 13:23, “leaning on Jesus' bosom.”
usage: “Lean not unto thine own understanding” — use it; do not rest your weight on it.
“Whereon if a man lean, it will go into his hand” — the world's help, honestly described by an Assyrian.
“Yet will they lean upon the LORD” — presumption dressed as trust.

pos: adj. and v. (bright, transparent; free of guilt; to acquit; rendering Hebrew naqah, zakah, and bar, Greek hagnos)
etymology: Latin clarus, bright, through Old French cler. The moral sense — clear of a charge — grows from the physical one: nothing in the way of the light.
biblical_def: The Name proclaimed to Moses ends with the word: the LORD is “forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty” (Exo 34:7). Judah, caught with the cup, asks, “how shall we clear ourselves? God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants” (Gen 44:16). David confesses so that God may “be clear when thou judgest” (Psa 51:4). Paul's Corinthians, having repented, “approved yourselves to be clear in this matter” (2Co 7:11). The bride is “clear as the sun” (Sng 6:10), the light of the city is “clear as crystal” (Rev 21:11), and the river of life proceeds from the throne “clear as crystal” (Rev 22:1). A servant released from an oath is “clear from this my oath” (Gen 24:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines clear as free from darkness or obscurity; transparent; free from guilt or blame; innocent; and, as a verb, to free from guilt, to acquit.
webster_full: CLEAR, a. Open; free from obstruction; free from clouds or darkness; bright; transparent.
2. Free from guilt or blame; innocent; unspotted; irreproachable.
3. Free from any thing that may be an impediment; free from debt or obligation.
CLEAR, v.t. To free from guilt or the imputation of guilt; to acquit; to justify.
scriptures: Exo 34:7

Keeping mercy for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, and that will by no means clear the guilty; visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, and upon the children's children, unto the third and to the fourth generation.
Psa 51:4
Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.

And Judah said, What shall we say unto my lord? what shall we speak? or how shall we clear ourselves? God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants: behold, we are my lord's servants, both we, and he also with whom the cup is found.
Rev 22:1
And he shewed me a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb.

For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge! In all things ye have approved yourselves to be clear in this matter.
Sng 6:10
Who is she that looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, and terrible as an army with banners?
corruption_summary: The Name is quoted as far as forgiving iniquity and cut off before by no means clearing the guilty.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 34:6–7 is the fullest self-description God gives in the Old Testament, and modern religion recites the first half of it. Merciful, gracious, longsuffering, abundant in goodness and truth, forgiving iniquity — and then the clause that is dropped: “that will by no means clear the guilty.” Both halves are the gospel. God forgives, and God does not acquit the guilty, and the cross is the one place where both are true of the same sinner at the same moment: “that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus” (Rom 3:26). Justification is not God clearing the guilty. It is God counting righteous those whose guilt has already been borne by Another.

Genesis 44:16 is the turn of the Joseph story. For twenty-two years the brothers have been clearing themselves; when the cup is found in Benjamin's sack Judah stops: “how shall we clear ourselves? God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants.” He is not speaking of the cup. Reconciliation begins where self-justification ends. David goes one step further in Psalm 51:4 and clears God instead of himself — “that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest” — which Paul quotes in Romans 3:4 as the posture of every true confession: let God be true, and every man a liar.

Second Corinthians 7:11 shows what a cleared conscience looks like from the outside. Godly sorrow wrought carefulness, clearing of themselves, indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, revenge — and by these the Corinthians “approved yourselves to be clear.” They were cleared by dealing with the matter, not by denying it. Cheap grace clears by forgetting; the apostolic church cleared by repenting.
roots_summary: Hebrew naqah (H5352), to be clean, acquitted, held innocent; zakah (H2135), to be pure, clear; tsadaq (H6663), to be just, to justify oneself; bar (H1249), pure, clear; Greek hagnos (G53), pure; krystallizo (G2929), to shine like crystal.
roots_lines: Hebrew naqah (H5352) — to be clean, acquitted, left unpunished; Exodus 34:7, Numbers 14:18, Genesis 24:8, Nahum 1:3.
Hebrew zakah (H2135) — to be clear, pure, justified; Psalm 51:4, Job 15:14, 25:4.
Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to be righteous, to justify oneself; Genesis 44:16, “how shall we clear ourselves?”
Greek hagnos (G53) — pure, clear; 2 Corinthians 7:11; and krystallizo (G2929), clear as crystal, Revelation 21:11.
usage: “Will by no means clear the guilty” — the half of the Name men forget.
“How shall we clear ourselves?” — the end of self-justification, and the beginning of reconciliation.
“Clear as crystal” — the river from the throne.

pos: adj. (of great heat; of wrath, kindled; of Laodicea's water, fervent; rendering Hebrew charah, cham, and chamam, Greek zestos)
etymology: Old English hāt. The Hebrew verbs of anger in the Old Testament are verbs of heat; wrath does not rise, it waxes hot.
biblical_def: Wrath is hot: “let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them” (Exo 32:10), and Moses answers, “LORD, why doth thy wrath wax hot against thy people?” (Exo 32:11). Manna melted “when the sun waxed hot” (Exo 16:21). Solomon asks, “Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?” (Pro 6:28). David's silence broke because “my heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned” (Psa 39:3). Ephraim's adulterers “are all hot as an oven” (Hos 7:7). And to Laodicea: “thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot. So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth” (Rev 3:15–16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hot as having sensible heat, opposed to cold; ardent in temper; violent; furious; vehement; eager.
webster_full: HOT, a. Having sensible heat; opposed to cold; as a hot stove or fire; a hot cloth; hot liquor.
2. Ardent in temper; easily excited or exasperated; vehement.
3. Violent; furious; as a hot engagement.
4. Eager; animated; brisk; keen; as a hot pursuit.
scriptures: Rev 3:15
I know thy works, that thou art neither cold nor hot: I would thou wert cold or hot.
Rev 3:16
So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.
Now therefore let me alone, that my wrath may wax hot against them, and that I may consume them: and I will make of thee a great nation.
Psa 39:3
My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue,
Pro 6:28
Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?
Hos 7:7
They are all hot as an oven, and have devoured their judges; all their kings are fallen: there is none among them that calleth unto me.
corruption_summary: Laodicea's hot and cold are read as zeal and hostility, which makes Christ prefer an enemy to a lukewarm friend.
corruption_paragraphs: The common reading of Revelation 3:15 has Christ wishing the Laodiceans were either on fire for Him or openly against Him, and then has to explain why He would prefer open hostility. He would not. The city's water is the picture: Hierapolis across the valley had hot springs, Colossae had cold ones, and Laodicea's supply arrived by aqueduct tepid and foul, fit only to be spat out. Hot water heals and cold water refreshes; both are useful, and lukewarm water is useful for nothing. The rebuke is uselessness. A church can be doctrinally respectable, financially comfortable (“I am rich, and increased with goods”), and good for nothing to anyone, and that is the church He threatens to spue out.

“My wrath may wax hot” is filed under the God of the Old Testament, as if Revelation 3:16 were a different temperature. It is the same heat in the mouth of the Lamb. Moses' intercession in Exodus 32 is worth watching for what it does not do: he never denies that the wrath is just. He pleads the covenant, the Name, and the fathers, and God repents of the evil. The intercessor who begins by explaining why the people did not deserve it has not read Moses.

Psalm 39:3 is the discipline of the heated heart. David resolved to keep silence “even from good,” his sorrow was stirred, his heart was hot within him, and the fire burned — “then spake I with my tongue.” He spoke to God. The verses that follow are prayer, not complaint to men, and the whole psalm is a model for what to do with a heart that has reached temperature: take it to the one hearer who can bear it.
roots_summary: Hebrew charah (H2734), to burn, be kindled (of anger); cham (H2525) and chamam (H2552), hot, to be hot; Greek zestos (G2200), boiling hot.
roots_lines: Hebrew charah (H2734) — to burn, to be kindled, of wrath; Exodus 32:10–11, 32:19, 22:24.
Hebrew chamam (H2552) — to be hot, grow warm; Psalm 39:3, Exodus 16:21, Hosea 7:7.
Hebrew cham (H2525) — hot, warm; Joshua 9:12, Job 37:17.
Greek zestos (G2200) — boiling hot; Revelation 3:15–16 only.
usage: “Neither cold nor hot” — Laodicea's useless water.
“That my wrath may wax hot” — and the intercessor did not deny it was just.
“My heart was hot within me” — a fire that found its outlet in prayer.

pos: n. (an interval of time or of distance; room; rendering Hebrew yamim and rachoq, Greek chronos and diastema)
etymology: Latin spatium, a stretch of room or time. In the Authorized Version the word is almost always an interval of time — a space of three years, of half an hour, to repent.
biblical_def: A space is a measured interval. Of time: “I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not” (Rev 2:21); “there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour” (Rev 8:1); Paul “by the space of three years” ceased not to warn the Ephesians night and day with tears (Act 20:31); Sapphira came in “about the space of three hours after” (Act 5:7); Ezra sees that “for a little space grace hath been shewed from the LORD our God” (Ezr 9:8). Of distance: at Jordan “there shall be a space between you and it, about two thousand cubits by measure: come not near unto it” (Jos 3:4). The beast “must continue a short space” (Rev 17:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines space as room; extension; a quantity of time; an interval between points or objects.
webster_full: SPACE, n. Room; extension; extent; capacity of being occupied.
2. Any quantity of extension; as, the space of a mile.
3. Quantity of time; also, an interval between two points of time; as, the space of a year.
4. A short time; a while.
scriptures: Rev 2:21
And I gave her space to repent of her fornication; and she repented not.
Ezr 9:8

And now for a little space grace hath been shewed from the LORD our God, to leave us a remnant to escape, and to give us a nail in his holy place, that our God may lighten our eyes, and give us a little reviving in our bondage.
Rev 8:1
And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven about the space of half an hour.
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
Jos 3:4
Yet there shall be a space between you and it, about two thousand cubits by measure: come not near unto it, that ye may know the way by which ye must go: for ye have not passed this way heretofore.
Act 5:7
And it was about the space of three hours after, when his wife, not knowing what was done, came in.
corruption_summary: God's delay is taken for God's indifference, when Scripture calls it space to repent and counts every unused day.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 2:21 is the anatomy of patience. Jezebel of Thyatira was given space to repent, and the sentence ends, “and she repented not.” The modern inference from delay is that God does not mind: the judgment has not come, therefore the thing was allowed. Peter answers that the longsuffering is “not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2Pe 3:9), and Paul answers what the unused space becomes — “despisest thou the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering… but after thy hardness and impenitent heart treasurest up unto thyself wrath” (Rom 2:4–5). Space to repent is evidence at the trial when it is not used.

Ezra 9:8 is what a man does with a little space of grace. The remnant has come back, the temple stands, God has given them “a nail in his holy place” — and Ezra's response to the season of favour is to tear his garment and confess the nation's sin. The corruption is the opposite reflex: taking a season of grace as an entitlement, and reading a quiet year as a verdict on one's righteousness. A little space is a loan.

Joshua 3:4 gives space its other direction. Two thousand cubits were to lie between the people and the ark — “come not near unto it” — so that every man could see the way, and so that the holy thing was not handled as common. Uzzah's hand closed the space and he died for it (2Sa 6:6–7). Reverence keeps a distance, and the modern familiarity with holy things, in which nothing is set apart and everything is within reach, is what Joshua 3 was built to prevent.
roots_summary: Hebrew yamim (H3117), days, a season; rachoq (H7350), a distance, far off; rega (H7281), a moment; Greek chronos (G5550), time; diastema (G1292), an interval; hemiorion (G2256), half an hour.
roots_lines: Hebrew yamim (H3117) — days, a period; Genesis 29:14, “the space of a month.”
Hebrew rachoq (H7350) — distance, far; Joshua 3:4, two thousand cubits.
Hebrew rega (H7281) — a moment, a little space; Ezra 9:8.
Greek chronos (G5550) — time, a season; Revelation 2:21, Acts 13:21; diastema (G1292), Acts 5:7; hemiorion (G2256), Revelation 8:1.
usage: “I gave her space to repent” — patience with a purpose, and a record of how it was spent.
“For a little space grace hath been shewed” — Ezra's season, and Ezra's confession.
“A space between you and it” — the distance reverence keeps.
